outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and Scope of Review
outline.description: This chapter establishes the procedural history of the case, identifying the parties, the specific forms of relief sought, and the decisions rendered by the Immigration Judge (IJ) and the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA). It defines the Tenth Circuit's jurisdictional basis and explains the highly deferential 'substantial evidence' standard applied to factual findings in asylum cases.
subtopics: Parties and Relief Sought: Asylum, Withholding of Removal, and CAT Claims
Administrative History: IJ Denial and BIA Affirmance
Scope of Appeal: Limiting Issues to Asylum and Withholding Grounds
Jurisdictional Basis under 8 U.S.C. § 1252
The Substantial Evidence Standard: When Facts Are Conclusive

outline.chapter_title: The Legal Framework for Asylum Eligibility
outline.description: This chapter outlines the statutory definition of a 'refugee' under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). It breaks down the three core elements an applicant must prove to establish eligibility based on past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution: the severity of harm, the nexus to a protected ground, and the role of state protection.
subtopics: Statutory Definition of a Refugee (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42))
Past Persecution vs. Well-Founded Fear of Future Persecution
The Rebuttable Presumption Arising from Past Persecution
The Three-Prong Test: Harm, Nexus, and State Control
Burden of Proof: Preponderance of the Evidence

outline.chapter_title: Analyzing the Severity of Harm: Why Threats Did Not Constitute Persecution
outline.description: This chapter examines the court's analysis of whether the petitioners' experiences rose to the level of 'persecution.' It contrasts the petitioners' allegations (threats, psychological distress, isolated intimidation) with Tenth Circuit precedent requiring severe suffering or harm, explaining why threats alone and uncorroborated psychological impacts were insufficient.
subtopics: Defining Persecution: More Than Restrictions or Sporadic Threats
The Cumulative Effect Doctrine vs. Isolated Incidents
Insufficiency of Threats Without Physical Harm or Detention
Psychological and Emotional Harm as Standalone Grounds for Persecution
Application to Facts: The Gunpoint Incident and School Harassment

outline.chapter_title: The Nexus Requirement: Political Opinion vs. Personal Vendetta
outline.description: This chapter details the court's reasoning regarding the 'nexus' element. It explains the 'one central reason' standard and analyzes how the court distinguished between harm caused by political opinion versus harm caused by interfering with criminal enterprise revenue. The chapter highlights why mixed-motive cases require proof that a protected ground was not merely tangential.
subtopics: The 'One Central Reason' Statutory Standard
Distinguishing Protected Grounds from Incidental Motives
Mixed-Motive Analysis in Asylum Jurisprudence
Fact Pattern Analysis: Campaign Activities vs. Property Dispute Interference
Evidence Linking Don Rafa to Criminal Revenue Protection Rather Than Politics

outline.chapter_title: State Protection and Internal Relocation Alternatives
outline.description: This chapter addresses the final barriers to relief: the government's ability/unwillingness to protect and the feasibility of internal relocation. It discusses the legal requirements for proving state complicity or futility in reporting crimes and evaluates why minimal contact with police and successful temporary relocation within Colombia defeated these arguments.
subtopics: 'Unable or Unwilling' Standard: Government Response Requirements
